Fischer had opened 1.e4 almost all his life, but two games ago he switched to 1.c4 and beat Spassky with it. He plays it again here, and the game reaches your line. Play your line, then try to find Fischer's moves.

Spassky died in 2025, aged 88.

Pushing the attack back
column5: In the Marshall, Black's queen, knight and bishop all aim at your king. Rh4 hits the queen and makes it leave h3. Once the attack stalls, White's extra pawn begins to count.

column4: Trade the attackers
column5: The f6 knight was holding Black's attack together. Ne4 swaps it off. Every trade helps the side that is a pawn up and under attack.

column4: The pin on the d-file
column5: The queen on d7 stands right behind the bishop on d6. Rd1 pins the bishop, and your bishops and queen can join in against it and against h7.

column4: Shut in
column5: c4 cuts the b3 bishop off from the rest of Black's pieces, and both Bxd6 and Bxh7+ are coming. Too many threats at once.

column3: Svidler resigned after 30.c4: he can't hold d6 and h7 at once. Polgar had taken the Marshall's pawn, survived the attack by pushing the queen back and trading pieces, and then won with a pin. Peter Leko won the tournament. That autumn Polgar became the first woman to play in a world championship tournament, in San Luis. She retired from competitive chess in 2014 and works to bring chess into schools.
